Chart system 01 · A concept for Board 3

Explainer

Explainer leads with the finding. Each chart opens with the kind of evidence and a sentence that says what the data shows, then a line that names the measure, unit, place and period. The drawing keeps one subject in Charcoal against Stone context, and notes inside the plot teach what a reader could otherwise miss. Charts sit in one reading column, the way an explainer runs, and four break wider where the data needs room. The scenario chart is a table, because a reader looks it up.

The working red appears once on this view, on the 2021 point that chart S02's title names.

S01 Big number in context

Reader question
Do Republicans and Democrats agree on anything about Congress?
Why this form
One large figure gives the fact a reader repeats; the party bars and the two votes put it in context in the same drawing.

Studio note, not part of the chart

S02 Line with event notes

Reader question
What happened to child poverty when the expanded child tax credit was paid, and after it lapsed?
Why this form
A line shows the rise and fall in order, and notes at 2021 and at the method breaks explain what a reader could misread.

Studio note, not part of the chart

S03 Ranked bar

Reader question
Who changed the rules: voters, courts or legislatures?
Why this form
Ranked bars answer who acted most, and splitting each bar by the atlas’s direction code shows which way each instrument moved the rules.

Studio note, not part of the chart

S04 Dot plot or dumbbell

Reader question
Which age groups vote, and did that change between two elections?
Why this form
A dumbbell puts two elections on one line for each age group, so the level and the change read at once.

Studio note, not part of the chart

S05 Small multiples

Reader question
How far apart are homeownership rates by race, and has the gap closed?
Why this form
Small multiples give each group its own panel on one scale, so a reader follows one line at a time and still sees the others.

Studio note, not part of the chart

S06 Comparison table

Reader question
If a reform path were followed, which way would each outcome move?
Why this form
A table lets a reader look up one scenario and one outcome; the atlas’s own words sit in every cell beside the studio’s arrow.

Studio note, not part of the chart

S07 Map

Reader question
Where can a city adopt ranked-choice voting, and where has the state ruled it out?
Why this form
A tile map gives each state the same weight, so the count reads true where a land map would favor large western states.

Studio note, not part of the chart

S08 Unit chart

Reader question
Have the rules been moving toward voters or away from them?
Why this form
One square per entry lets a reader count, and placing toward above the year line and away below it shows the turn without a second chart.

Studio note, not part of the chart

S09 Timeline

Reader question
Which rule changes since 1870 decided who counts, who governs, who owns and who checks?
Why this form
A true time scale shows when changes bunch together, and four lanes keep each thread readable.

Studio note, not part of the chart

S10 Evidence mix

Reader question
How much of each everyday answer rests on documented fact?
Why this form
A bar split by grade shows how much of each answer rests on the record, and sorting by that share puts the answers in order.

Chart system 01 · Explainer

On Newsprint

The same ten charts from the same generators, with the ground changed. Gridlines take Stone mixed 70 percent toward Newsprint, secondary text stays in Deep Stone, which measures 5.49:1 here where Stone measures 4.29:1, and any text on a light fill turns Charcoal. Pillar Red measures 2.96:1 on Newsprint, under the 3:1 a mark needs, so the one red point takes a 1 px Charcoal keyline.

Chart system 01 · Explainer

On Charcoal

Two charts with the proposed dark palette. Newsprint carries the subject; Dim Newsprint carries secondary text; context lines take Stone mixed 35 percent toward Newsprint; gridlines drop to Stone mixed 45 percent toward Charcoal. On Charcoal, lifted Prussian and lifted Verdigris land too close to tell apart, so dark charts keep to few categories and label every series directly. The grade ramp steps from Newsprint to Stone mixed 35 percent toward Newsprint, then Stone, then a hatch, so it keeps its order by lightness.

Chart system 01 · Explainer

Social card

One chart as a portrait post at 1080 by 1350 pixels, the size Instagram and LinkedIn use. It is chart S01 from the same generator, with type at one and a quarter times its page size so labels hold at a phone's feed width. The card keeps the evidence label, the title, the measure line, the source and the wordmark, so it still makes sense when it travels without the page. It sits on Newsprint, the ground a feed of white cards does not use.

Anatomy of a chart

Chart S02 with every part numbered. The red point here is a specimen, so it does not count toward this view’s red.

1

Finding

Official statistic: Census Bureau survey estimates

2Child poverty fell to 5.1 percent in 2021, the lowest since the series began in 2009, and more than doubled the next year.

3Children under 18 below the Supplemental Poverty Measure, percent, United States, 2009 to 2025, with the official measure in gray for comparison

13Source: U.S. Census Bureau, Poverty in the United States: 2025 (P60-290), Table 8, Supplemental Poverty Measure, children under 18, 2009 to 2025, United States. Retrieved November 6, 2026. Figures for 2019 to 2024 include the Bureau’s August 2026 revision and differ by up to 0.4 points from those first published.

Chart: Oath & Action

14Show the table and notes

  1. Evidence label. The kind of evidence in a Charcoal chip: Finding, Association, Estimate or Illustration. The grade follows in words.
  2. Title. One sentence that states the finding, in Inter Tight 800. Its verb matches the grade: record words for documented, “can” or “may” for plausible, “would” for a scenario.
  3. Measure line. The measure, unit, place and period, in Inter 400 Deep Stone. It says when a scale is cropped.
  4. Unit on the top tick. The unit appears once, on the top tick or the first label. Other ticks stay bare.
  5. Gridlines. Horizontal 1 px hairlines in the grid tint. No vertical grid and no tick marks.
  6. Baseline. A 1.5 px Charcoal line at zero. Bars always start here.
  7. Subject. The series the title names: 3 px Charcoal, labeled directly in Inter 600.
  8. Context. Other series in 2 px Stone, labeled in Deep Stone. They recede so the subject reads first.
  9. The one red point. Pillar Red marks only the point the title names, once per view. On Newsprint it takes a 1 px Charcoal keyline.
  10. Note and leader. Notes sit inside the drawing in Inter 14 px Deep Stone, joined to the data by a 1 px leader.
  11. Odd encoding, explained once. Here the steps at 2013, 2017 and 2019 are method breaks. The line never bridges them.
  12. End note. A note in open space names the value a reader would look for, with a leader to the point.
  13. Source line and credit. Publisher, table, period, geography, date retrieved and the qualification, in that order. The credit sits at right.
  14. Table and notes. One click opens every value and every note, so the chart has a full equivalent.

Type

The locked faces only. Inter Tight sets titles and big numbers, Inter sets every label and number with tabular figures and a true minus (−), and Lora Italic appears only for quoted words. Nothing on screen goes under 13 px; phone drawings set nothing under 14 px so they hold 13 px on a 320 px phone.

Marks

Line weights follow the studio’s family of 1, 1.5, 2, 3 and 6 px (D2-60).

Color, measured on each ground

Every chart color is a role, and every tint is an OKLab mix of locked colors with one job. Contrast is measured against the ground (WCAG 2.x). Text needs 4.5:1; a mark needs 3:1; a fill under 3:1 is used only where every value is printed or the table carries it, which is a design judgment. Categories never rest on Verdigris against Stone alone: they sit 0.05 apart in OKLab lightness, so position or a label carries them too.

Notes and source lines

Notes in the drawing

  • Name the record, give a reader’s scale, or explain an unusual encoding once. A note that does none of these comes out.
  • Put the note in open space near its data and join it with a 1 px Stone leader. Leaders run straight or with one bend, never across a label.
  • Notes are Inter 14 px in Deep Stone; a note head that states a number is Inter 600 in Charcoal.
  • State the qualification in the drawing when it changes the reading: self-reported rates, method breaks, a survey older than the votes.
  • A note may say what a measure did over time. It never says a policy caused it unless the source grades that cause.
  • Label series at the line or the bar. Use a key only when labels cannot fit, and draw the key in the chart’s own marks.

Source lines

  • Order: publisher, title or table, observation period, geography, date retrieved, qualification (Master Brief section 15).
  • Start from the dataset’s source line. Shorten only by dropping words, never facts. Dates read as words: October 15, 2026.
  • Inter 400, 13/18, Deep Stone, under a grid-tint hairline, with “Chart: Oath & Action” at the right.
  • A secondary source says so in the line, as the ranked-choice map does for Ballotpedia.
  • The table under every chart repeats the source, so the equivalent stands on its own.

Red, once

Rule 05.3, as Dustin approved it (D2-01):

“The wordmark’s ampersand and the lockmark’s lever are signature red and do not count, and neither do the ampersands inside the hinge diagram and the hinge-circle badge, which are identity marks. The hinge diagram never shares a view with the wordmark and never stands in for the hinge divider. An icon’s red accent counts as signature red when the icon stands alone, as an app tile, an avatar or a single feature icon. In a row or a menu, icons go one color and only the current one keeps its red. Each view (one screen, card, slide or printed page) then carries one working red, in this order of precedence: an error the reader must fix; the step a reader can take now; the one point the headline names, which in a systems figure is where a reform acts. One job may take several marks, such as each target of one reform. A hinge headline’s ampersand uses the view’s working red. The hinge divider’s ampersand takes its surface’s ink: Charcoal on Newsprint and White, Newsprint on Charcoal, White on Prussian. In the guide itself, specimens, labeled failure cases and palette swatches do not count. Red never sits on Prussian.”

On a chart page each chart counts as one view. In this concept the working red goes to one chart per page view, S02, on the point its title names. Party marks, grades, scales and categories never take red.

Demonstration A, a specimen: red marks the point the title names

With nothing else in the view asking for red, the 2021 low takes it. Red points; it never encodes a series.

Demonstration B, a specimen: an ask takes the red, and the point steps down

Find your state’s child poverty rate

The step a reader can take now outranks the point the title names, so the ask keeps the red and the 2021 point turns Charcoal with a ground-colored ring to hold it apart from the line.

How to read our charts

For readers, in plain words. This text can run under any chart or on a help page.

  1. Start with the label. The black chip says what kind of evidence the chart shows. A Finding is something measured. An Association is a pattern that does not show one thing caused another. An Estimate says what would happen if something else happened first. An Illustration shows how a chart works, with made-up numbers.
  2. Read the title as the answer. It is one sentence that says what the numbers show. If the title says “would” or “may,” the evidence is less certain.
  3. Check what was counted. The gray line under the title names what was measured, in what unit, where and when.
  4. Look for the dark line. The black line, bar or dot is what the title is about. Gray marks are there for comparison.
  5. Read the notes in the chart. Short notes point at the record, the turning point or anything drawn in an unusual way, such as a line that breaks where a survey changed.
  6. Red points at one thing. When a chart uses red, it marks the single point the title names. Red never means a party, good or bad.
  7. Find where the numbers came from. The source line names who collected the data, when, and what to keep in mind. Open the table to see every value.

Data: Who Do They Answer To? Systems Atlas V7, snapshot October 15, 2026, and public series from the U.S. Census Bureau and Ballotpedia retrieved November 6, 2026. Every chart is drawn by a generator in build_concept.py.

Chart system 01, Explainer. Studio draft for Board 3; titles and notes are drafts by the studio.
